title: Expressive Speech — Stress and Intonation
learningGoals: Choose what matters in a sentence
Use comfortable melody in your own voice

sections.heading: Welcome and what we will explore
sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Expressive Speech — Stress and Intonation. You say the right words, but the part you care about is lost because every word receives the same weight.

We will hear how emphasis changes meaning, choose what matters in a sentence, and use comfortable melody in your own voice. First I will explain the distinction. Then you will see and hear a demonstration, try a few short phrases, and notice your own experience. We will finish with a short prepared rehearsal and an everyday next step. You can pause or ask a question at any point. A small comfortable experiment is enough.

sections.heading: What this tool means
sections.narration:
Stress is the emphasis given to a word or part of a word. Intonation is the pitch movement across an utterance. Both can express meaning. You can explore a small contrast comfortably, including at a slower pace; the task is not to perform a dramatic voice.

The same words can communicate different meanings through emphasis and melody. We will explore expression without turning your voice into an impression of somebody else. Start from what you mean. Let the important part receive attention, then return to a natural explanation in your own voice. Expression is available at a slower pace too.

Notice the distinction: Meaning guides the choice. Expression does not require imitating another speaker or maximizing pitch movement. You are choosing one feature for this learning experience, rather than inspecting every aspect of speech. We will use short familiar messages so there is room to notice that feature.

sections.heading: Watch and listen
sections.narration:
Watch the demonstration before trying. We will use this message: I wanted the blue one. First listen to the models and notice the feature being compared. The labels on screen identify each version. You can replay either model without copying an uncomfortable contrast.

Now listen once more for the message itself. Meaning, expression, comfort and whether the listener can hear the intended emphasis. This is an invitation to compare your experience, not a demand to match the model exactly. When you are ready, move to a short guided attempt.

sections.heading: Try the three small steps
sections.narration:
Let us try this in small steps. First: Choose what matters in a short sentence. Next: Say it with emphasis that matches the intention. Then: Use natural melody in a short story or explanation.

Use these familiar phrases one at a time: I wanted the blue one. Are you coming with us? That was the part I enjoyed most. Stop between attempts when you want to. You can listen to a model again, record a short attempt, or leave this part to return later. Keep attention on this one chosen feature; you do not need to check every sound. If the attempt becomes effortful, stop and return to comfortable ordinary speaking.

sections.heading: Compare and check
sections.narration:
Consider what this tool is asking you to explore. What should guide emphasis? You can select an answer and read or hear the explanation. It is a check of the idea, not a test of how you sound.

After the check, notice one observation from your attempt: Meaning, expression, comfort and whether the listener can hear the intended emphasis. It is possible for a movement to feel different while the message still takes effort, or for you to be unsure what changed. You can record that uncertainty without repeating until you obtain a preferred result.

sections.heading: From a phrase to your own message
sections.narration:
Choose a short message you actually want to share. You might use one of the phrases we have practised and add one useful detail in your own words. Give yourself one small cue from the demonstration, then let the message continue. There is no need to increase the amount of the technique to make the attempt count.

After speaking, ask what you noticed about the chosen feature and about the message. You can keep a small useful change, adjust it, or leave the result open. Try another short message only if it serves your learning today.

sections.heading: Your observation and next step
sections.narration:
Before finishing, save one observation. Here is the feature we explored: Meaning, expression, comfort and whether the listener can hear the intended emphasis. Something may have changed, things may have felt much the same, or you may be unsure. Your observation belongs to this attempt and setting.

In focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one feature. In conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; it does not need to become a checklist you monitor throughout the exchange.

Choose one manageable situation in which you would like to speak. You can plan a small practice, have a conversation, revisit the demonstration, or finish here. Save what you would keep, change or leave open.
